items.title: NASA JPL Looks to Next 90 Years of Innovation, Exploration

extraData.description: Interstellar probes. Lunar drones. Helicopters on Mars. extraData.dc:creator: Amanda Barnett
extraData.content:encoded:
5 min read

Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater)

Interstellar probes. Lunar drones. Helicopters on Mars.

When a group of Caltech graduate students and enthusiasts began conducting rocket-propulsion tests in PasadenaGÇÖs Arroyo Seco on Oct. 31, 1936, they had no idea that their work marked the inception of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Ninety years later, the lab, now managed by Caltech for NASA, isnGÇÖt only celebrating the long line of historic firsts accomplished here; itGÇÖs paving the way for many to come.

Initially a contractor for the U.S. Army, JPL launched AmericaGÇÖs first satellite, Explorer 1 in 1958. But rather than just orbiting Earth like the Soviet UnionGÇÖs Sputnik, Explorer 1 became the first spacecraft to conduct science, thanks to an onboard Geiger counter that discovered the protective radiation belts encircling Earth.

The lab joined part of the newly formed NASA that same year. Within six years, in 1964, JPL sent the first U.S. mission to the Moon, Ranger 7. It also went on to lead the first planetary flyby, the first probe to visit all four gas giants, the first infrared telescope, the first rovers to roll on Mars, and the first rotorcraft to fly there, among many other historic milestones.

More firsts are on the way.

GÇ£Over the course of 90 years, JPLGÇÖs first-of-a-kind missions have transformed our understanding of the universe and our place in it,GÇ¥ said Dave Gallagher, JPLGÇÖs director since 2025. In 1992, only a couple years after he started as an engineer at the lab, Gallagher led the JPL team that built and tested the Wide-Field and Planetary 2 Camera for NASAGÇÖs Hubble Space Telescope, which delivered many of the missionGÇÖs most iconic images. GÇ£We stand on an extraordinary foundation, and weGÇÖre ready to push the boundaries with exciting new missions so that future generations can go even further.GÇ¥

Aiming for a 2028 launch, the JPL-managed SkyFall mission will deploy three helicopters mid-descent over Mars to search to map hidden ice deposits and analyze weather patterns. Helping advance NASAGÇÖs Moon Base, JPL is developing MoonFall, a mission that will land a group of large propulsive drones at the lunar South Pole that same year. Set for a 2027 launch, SunRISE (Sun Radio Interferometer Space Experiment) features six toaster-oven-size satellites that will fly in formation to create a miles-wide radio antenna dish in order to study the SunGÇÖs activity. What it reveals could help make space exploration safer for humans.

Protecting humanity is also the goal of the asteroid-hunting NEO Surveyor (Near-Earth Object Surveyor) mission, which, managed by JPL, will hunt for potentially hazardous space rocks that other telescopes canGÇÖt find. Once an object is spotted, NASA can offer a threat assessment and plan accordingly.

Closer to home, the same lab that launched the first oceanographic satellite in 1978 is at work on several missions that will offer a deeper reading of EarthGÇÖs vital signs. Where one mission will monitor the movement of water by measuring slight changes in gravity, another will study how powerful tropical convective storms form. A third will detail how different types of air pollution affect human health.

They add to a fleet of other Earth missions and projects JPL helps lead, including NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) a joint mission with the Indian Space Research Organisation that can pinpoint how EarthGÇÖs surface changes in relation to natural disasters. Another, one of a series of instruments called AVIRIS (Airborne Visible Infrared Imaging Spectrometer), can even detect rare Earth elements critical to modern technology.

Flown on airplanes, the AVIRIS sensors were developed at JPLGÇÖs Microdevices Laboratory, which invented the GÇ£camera on a chipGÇ¥ technology that enables cellphones to take pictures. ItGÇÖs also where the detectors are being developed for PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics), a newly announced NASA mission that will strengthen humanityGÇÖs understanding of the universe by studying radiant energy visible only in the far-infrared.

GÇ£Bringing together the very best of scientific brilliance and engineering ingenuity from across Caltech and JPL continues to advance NASAGÇÖs priorities and empower AmericaGÇÖs space leadership,GÇ¥ said CaltechGÇÖs president Ray Jayawardhana, who is also a professor of astronomy. GÇ£I can only imagine what those Caltech students experimenting with rockets in a little patch of dry riverbed would think if they could to see what Caltech and JPL have accomplished since, and where weGÇÖre headed next. Ninety years later, the same spirit of daring is still opening new frontiers and inspiring humanity.GÇ¥

The 90th anniversary comes just a few weeks before another milestone, when on Nov. 18 Voyager 1 reaches a full light-day GÇö the distance light will travel in 24 hours, which is some 16 billion miles, or 26 billion kilometers GÇö from Earth. Ed Stone led the mission for 50 years, serving as JPLGÇÖs director for 10 of them. Stone died in 2024, but the Voyagers are continuing on their journey deeper into interstellar space, a place no other spacecraft have ventured. Turning 50 next year, they rely on NASAGÇÖs Deep Space Network (developed by JPL in the Apollo era) to receive commands and send back science data. Stone said that with both Voyagers exploring regions never before visited, GÇ£every day is a day of discovery.GÇ¥ The same could be said for JPL.

-end-

GÇ£Over the course of 90 years, JPLGÇÖs first-of-a-kind missions have transformed our understanding of the universe and our place in it,GÇ¥ said Dave Gallagher, JPLGÇÖs director since 2025. In 1992, only a couple years after he started as an engineer at the lab, Gallagher led the JPL team that built and tested the Wide-Field and Planetary 2 Camera for NASAGÇÖs Hubble Space Telescope, which delivered many of the missionGÇÖs most iconic images. GÇ£We stand on an extraordinary foundation, and weGÇÖre ready to push the boundaries with exciting new missions so that future generations can go even further.GÇ¥

Aiming for a 2028 launch, the JPL-managed SkyFall mission will deploy three helicopters mid-descent over Mars to search to map hidden ice deposits and analyze weather patterns. Helping advance NASAGÇÖs Moon Base, JPL is developing MoonFall, a mission that will land a group of large propulsive drones at the lunar South Pole that same year. Set for a 2027 launch, SunRISE (Sun Radio Interferometer Space Experiment) features six toaster-oven-size satellites that will fly in formation to create a miles-wide radio antenna dish in order to study the SunGÇÖs activity. What it reveals could help make space exploration safer for humans.

Protecting humanity is also the goal of the asteroid-hunting NEO Surveyor (Near-Earth Object Surveyor) mission, which, managed by JPL, will hunt for potentially hazardous space rocks that other telescopes canGÇÖt find. Once an object is spotted, NASA can offer a threat assessment and plan accordingly.

Closer to home, the same lab that launched the first oceanographic satellite in 1978 is at work on several missions that will offer a deeper reading of EarthGÇÖs vital signs. Where one mission will monitor the movement of water by measuring slight changes in gravity, another will study how powerful tropical convective storms form. A third will detail how different types of air pollution affect human health.

They add to a fleet of other Earth missions and projects JPL helps lead, including NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) a joint mission with the Indian Space Research Organisation that can pinpoint how EarthGÇÖs surface changes in relation to natural disasters. Another, one of a series of instruments called AVIRIS (Airborne Visible Infrared Imaging Spectrometer), can even detect rare Earth elements critical to modern technology.

Flown on airplanes, the AVIRIS sensors were developed at JPLGÇÖs Microdevices Laboratory, which invented the GÇ£camera on a chipGÇ¥ technology that enables cellphones to take pictures. ItGÇÖs also where the detectors are being developed for PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics), a newly announced NASA mission that will strengthen humanityGÇÖs understanding of the universe by studying radiant energy visible only in the far-infrared.-á

GÇ£Bringing together the very best of scientific brilliance and engineering ingenuity from across Caltech and JPL continues to advance NASAGÇÖs priorities and empower AmericaGÇÖs space leadership,GÇ¥ said CaltechGÇÖs president Ray Jayawardhana, who is also a professor of astronomy. GÇ£I can only imagine what those Caltech students experimenting with rockets in a little patch of dry riverbed would think if they could to see what Caltech and JPL have accomplished since, and where weGÇÖre headed next. Ninety years later, the same spirit of daring is still opening new frontiers and inspiring humanity.GÇ¥

The 90th anniversary comes just a few weeks before another milestone, when on Nov. 18 Voyager 1 reaches a full light-day GÇö the distance light will travel in 24 hours, which is some 16 billion miles, or 26 billion kilometers GÇö from Earth. Ed Stone led the mission for 50 years, serving as JPLGÇÖs director for 10 of them. Stone died in 2024, but the Voyagers are continuing on their journey deeper into interstellar space, a place no other spacecraft have ventured. Turning 50 next year, they rely on NASAGÇÖs Deep Space Network (developed by JPL in the Apollo era) to receive commands and send back science data. Stone said that with both Voyagers exploring regions never before visited, GÇ£every day is a day of discovery.GÇ¥ The same could be said for JPL.

-end-

extraData.content:encoded:
As part of the agencyGÇÖs Inspiration Tour, NASA will conduct a flyover at the University of Alabama vs. Texas A&M football game in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, on Saturday, Oct. 24. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman will pilot one of three F-5 fighter jets during the flyover, highlighting NASA’s contributions to aeronautics and the agency’s continued commitment to advancing aviation technologies.

Ahead of the game, members of the news media are invited to visit the NASA Experience Zone on Champions Lane, where Isaacman will participate in a media opportunity at 11 a.m. CDT. Media interested in attending should confirm their attendance by 12 p.m. Friday, Oct. 23, with Lance D. Davis at lance.d.davis@nasa.gov to receive additional details and instructions.

Supported by NASAGÇÖs Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, the NASA Experience Zone will be open to the public from 10:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. CDT, with no game ticket required. The experience will give visitors an opportunity to meet NASA team members and learn more about the people and technologies advancing the agencyGÇÖs missions in aeronautics and space exploration.

Attendees can engage with NASA team members and explore exhibits highlighting the agency’s Artemis campaign and efforts to return astronauts to the Moon, including:

  • An inflatable SLS (Space Launch System) rocket.
  • Displays featuring the Starship and Blue Moon human landing systems.
  • Information about NASA internship opportunities.
  • Photo opportunities featuring NASA exhibits and displays.

With stops across the nation, NASAGÇÖs Inspiration Tour convenes academic, industry, and public sector stakeholders to connect the agency with the people, technologies, and organizations that drive American leadership in space.

The tour will culminate in MAX POWER, a public exposition of American air and space innovation, Saturday, Nov. 7, and Sunday, Nov. 8, on and near the agencyGÇÖs Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Held in honor of AmericaGÇÖs historic 250th anniversary, the multi-day, family-friendly event will showcase the next-generation aircraft, spacecraft, autonomous vehicles, and technologies that will help define the future of transportation in air and space. 

For more information about MAX POWER and the agencyGÇÖs missions, visit:

https://www.nasa.gov/maxpower

-end-

Written by Vandi Verma, Chief Engineer for Robotic Operations at NASAGÇÖs Jet Propulsion Laboratory

Oct. 12, 2026

Since the last blog update, Perseverance has achieved a major milestone on Mars. On Sol 2006 (Oct. 11, 2026), its odometer reached 45.22 kilometers (28.10 miles), setting a new record for the farthest distance driven on another celestial body. Its engineering twin here on Earth even received a plaque from Guinness World Records celebrating the achievement.

Two months ago, on Sol 1947, the odometer sat about 200 meters away from the milestone, a distance easily achievable with a single drive using Autonomous Navigation (AutoNav). However, the rover found itself in a very scientifically interesting area and spent time executing short drives to perform rock abrasions and proximity science on ancient rock outcrops. When Perseverance was finally ready to move on to a new site, it sailed past the record.

On its way to the drive record, Perseverance has navigated challenging terrain while also pioneering new ways to drive across the Martian surface. PerseveranceGÇÖs various encounters with dense boulder fields and steep slopes have pushed the team to re-evaluate driving guidelines so the rover is better prepared to handle tough terrain. After running thousands of simulations, the team raised the roverGÇÖs tilt limit to 24 degrees and reduced the clearance required under the roverGÇÖs belly pan to 20 centimeters (about 7.9 inches). The team also updated the roverGÇÖs braking software to avoid rock hazards, nearly doubled steer motor current limits, updated flight software with GÇ£dynamic slip tablesGÇ¥ to model expected slip, and used cross-slope driving to better anchor wheels on exposed bedrock.

One of the most exciting updates the team has made is an autonomous drive capability called onboard Global Localization (GBLC). GBLC repurposes the high-speed commercial processor inside the Ingenuity Helicopter Base Station to compare ground and orbital imagery to autonomously locate the rover in global coordinates at the end of a drive (as though we had GPS on a world without it), enabling Perseverance to drive longer distances without human intervention. Unlike PerseveranceGÇÖs main flight computer, this coprocessor is not hardened against the punishing radiation environment of the Martian surface, where a thin atmosphere and the lack of a global magnetosphere leave little shielding. This radiation can induce GÇ£transient bit flipsGÇ¥ in memory the software needs to function, and the team developed an effective software-based approach to radiation hardening. Looking forward to the greater demands of longer drives and to planning more activity with fewer resources, the team is also exploring the use of generative SI to help efficiently propose solutions to steer AutoNav along the many legs of a strategic path.

The team is using hard-won lessons from 45 kilometers (more than 28 miles) of driving to reinvent how the rover drives across the Martian surface. As Perseverance climbs higher along the crater rim, the next leap in autonomous exploration on Mars is just getting started.

From orbit, todayGÇÖs space-based laser instruments measure EarthGÇÖs forests and terrain one narrow line at a time. Between those lines are enormous gaps that include millions of acres of land scientists never directly measure. NASAGÇÖs CASALS instrument will blend machine learning with an ultra-compact lidar instrument to adaptively GÇÿsweepGÇÖ large swaths of EarthGÇÖs surface. This new capability for space-based remote sensors allows CASALS to create truly three-dimensional (3D) topographical renderings.

Video from a CASALS flight over the Great Cypress Swamp in Delaware on Nov. 12, 2024, showing tree canopy tops in green, the ground in purple, and near-ground vegetation in blue.
Credit: NASA

A team of researchers at NASAGÇÖs Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) has developed a new instrument designed to eliminate blind spots between lines of lidar data on the EarthGÇÖs surface. Built with support from NASAGÇÖs Earth Science Technology Office (ESTO), the Concurrent Artificially-intelligent Spectrometry Lidar System (CASALS) could help researchers map the features of EarthGÇÖs surface with unprecedented detail. Rather than mechanically steering a laser with moving mirrors, CASALS steers light using wavelength itself, generating a continuous, 3D swath of the ground below.

John Yorks, a physical research scientist at GSFC and Principal Investigator for CASALS, explained that the instrument features a novel transmitter and optical grating system that manipulates laser pulses without heavy, failure-prone motorized mirrors.

Instead, CASALS uses a fast-pulsing, tunable GÇ£seedGÇ¥ laser centered at 1040 nanometers, rapidly cycling through 256 unique wavelengths as it pulses through an optical component with a microscopic pattern of ridges called a transmission grating.

At this point, the physics of diffraction takes over. Because light bends at slightly different angles depending on its exact wavelength, the grating naturally GÇ£steersGÇ¥ each of the 256 pulses into a distinct position across the flight path.

This non-mechanical approach paints a continuous 3D swath of the ground. Not only does this eliminate the large unmapped gaps left between the isolated tracks of legacy spaceborne lidars, but stripping away moving parts drastically reduces the instrumentGÇÖs size, weight, and power (SWaP) requirements. This makes it more reliable for the harsh environment of space.

Another key innovation within CASALS is its detector array. This component features a uniquely high Quantum Efficiency (QE), a variable that describes how effectively a detector converts incoming light (photons) into an electrical signal. CASALS operates at 80% QE. This means CASALS wastes almost none of the light that makes it back to the sensor.

With QE that high, CASALS can detect much weaker return signals, allowing it to collect useful measurements from darker surfaces or through denser vegetation.

This technology isnGÇÖt limited to a laboratory environment. In November 2024, an airborne CASALS prototype flew aboard NASAGÇÖs B200 King Air aircraft. The instrument produced science-quality datasets on its first campaign, exceeding the teamGÇÖs expectations.

GÇ£IGÇÖm very impressed with Guang Yang, Jeffrey Chen, and all our engineers, and how well CASALS performed. This worked really well from the first time we flew it, which is pretty impressive,GÇ¥ said Yorks.

Flying at an altitude of roughly five kilometers, CASALS can distinguish individual tree branches and subtle changes in ground elevation, thanks to its 22-centimeter horizontal resolution.

GÇ£WeGÇÖre able to see really fine details of vegetation structure and changes in the topography of the surface,GÇ¥ Yorks said.

The team aims to fly CASALS again as part of the Airborne Surface, Cryosphere, Ecosystem, and Nearshore Topography (ASCENT) campaign, scheduled for summer 2027.

But thereGÇÖs more work to do to prepare the technology for space. The team plans to make several improvements to CASALS before creating a space-ready prototype. Specifically, theyGÇÖre widening the instrumentGÇÖs swath and adding onboard data processing software.

Transitioning from a successful airborne prototype to a fully realized space mission is a challenge, but the CASALS team is up to the task.

GÇ£The teamGÇÖs really done a great job of sticking together and keeping on task and on schedule. We are being funded to optimize and improve the performance, and weGÇÖre also then looking at ways to take the technologies used in the airborne instrument and mature them and prepare them for a spaceborne version in the future,GÇ¥ said Yorks.

If successful, CASALS could become the first spaceborne lidar capable of mapping EarthGÇÖs forests and terrain as continuous three-dimensional swaths rather than isolated profiles, giving scientists a dramatically more complete picture of our changing planet.

For additional details, see the entry for this project on NASA TechPort.

Project Lead(s): John Yorks, NASAGÇÖs Goddard Space Flight Center

Sponsoring Organization(s): NASAGÇÖs Decadal Survey Incubation (DSI) program; NASAGÇÖs Instrument Incubation Program (IIP); NASAGÇÖs Goddard Space Flight Center; University of California, Santa Barbara; Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University

• Overview

From orbit, todayGÇÖs space-based laser instruments measure EarthGÇÖs forests and terrain one narrow line at a time. Between those lines are enormous gaps that include millions of acres of land scientists never directly measure. NASAGÇÖs CASALS instrument will blend machine learning with an ultra-compact lidar instrument to adaptively GÇÿsweepGÇÖ large swaths of EarthGÇÖs surface. This new capability for space-based remote sensors allows CASALS to create truly three-dimensional (3D) topographical renderings.-á

Video from a CASALS flight over the Great Cypress Swamp in Delaware on Nov. 12, 2024, showing tree canopy tops in green, the ground in purple, and near-ground vegetation in blue.
Credit: NASA

A team of researchers at NASAGÇÖs Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) has developed a new instrument designed to eliminate blind spots between lines of lidar data on the EarthGÇÖs surface. Built with support from NASAGÇÖs Earth Science Technology Office (ESTO), the Concurrent Artificially-intelligent Spectrometry Lidar System (CASALS) could help researchers map the features of EarthGÇÖs surface with unprecedented detail. Rather than mechanically steering a laser with moving mirrors, CASALS steers light using wavelength itself, generating a continuous, 3D swath of the ground below.-á

John Yorks, a physical research scientist at GSFC and Principal Investigator for CASALS, explained that the instrument features a novel transmitter and optical grating system that manipulates laser pulses without heavy, failure-prone motorized mirrors.-á

Instead, CASALS uses a fast-pulsing, tunable GÇ£seedGÇ¥ laser centered at 1040 nanometers, rapidly cycling through 256 unique wavelengths as it pulses through an optical component with a microscopic pattern of ridges called a transmission grating.-á

At this point, the physics of diffraction takes over. Because light bends at slightly different angles depending on its exact wavelength, the grating naturally GÇ£steersGÇ¥ each of the 256 pulses into a distinct position across the flight path.-á

This non-mechanical approach paints a continuous 3D swath of the ground. Not only does this eliminate the large unmapped gaps left between the isolated tracks of legacy spaceborne lidars, but stripping away moving parts drastically reduces the instrumentGÇÖs size, weight, and power (SWaP) requirements. This makes it more reliable for the harsh environment of space.-á

Another key innovation within CASALS is its detector array. This component features a uniquely high Quantum Efficiency (QE), a variable that describes how effectively a detector converts incoming light (photons) into an electrical signal. CASALS operates at 80% QE. This means CASALS wastes almost none of the light that makes it back to the sensor.-á

With QE that high, CASALS can detect much weaker return signals, allowing it to collect useful measurements from darker surfaces or through denser vegetation.-á

This technology isnGÇÖt limited to a laboratory environment. In November 2024, an airborne CASALS prototype flew aboard NASAGÇÖs B200 King Air aircraft. The instrument produced science-quality datasets on its first campaign, exceeding the teamGÇÖs expectations.-á

GÇ£IGÇÖm very impressed with Guang Yang, Jeffrey Chen, and all our engineers, and how well CASALS performed. This worked really well from the first time we flew it, which is pretty impressive,GÇ¥ said Yorks.-á

Flying at an altitude of roughly five kilometers, CASALS can distinguish individual tree branches and subtle changes in ground elevation, thanks to its 22-centimeter horizontal resolution.-á

GÇ£WeGÇÖre able to see really fine details of vegetation structure and changes in the topography of the surface,GÇ¥ Yorks said.-á

The team aims to fly CASALS again as part of the Airborne Surface, Cryosphere, Ecosystem, and Nearshore Topography (ASCENT) campaign, scheduled for summer 2027.-á

But thereGÇÖs more work to do to prepare the technology for space. The team plans to make several improvements to CASALS before creating a space-ready prototype. Specifically, theyGÇÖre widening the instrumentGÇÖs swath and adding onboard data processing software.-á

Transitioning from a successful airborne prototype to a fully realized space mission is a challenge, but the CASALS team is up to the task.-á

GÇ£The teamGÇÖs really done a great job of sticking together and keeping on task and on schedule. We are being funded to optimize and improve the performance, and weGÇÖre also then looking at ways to take the technologies used in the airborne instrument and mature them and prepare them for a spaceborne version in the future,GÇ¥ said Yorks.-á

If successful, CASALS could become the first spaceborne lidar capable of mapping EarthGÇÖs forests and terrain as continuous three-dimensional swaths rather than isolated profiles, giving scientists a dramatically more complete picture of our changing planet.-á

For additional details, see the entry for this project on NASA TechPort.-á

Astronomy Picture of the Day

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

New Ghosts Revealed in Cassiopeia

Explanation: Jinkies, look at all those ghosts! It took 100 hours of observation and a special oxygen filter for todayGÇÖs image to capture three faint nebulas hidden in the Cassiopeia constellation. IC 59 and IC 63, the original Ghosts of Cassiopeia, haunt the region near multi-star system +¦ Cassiopeia. Energetic light from +¦ Cassiopeia causes the hydrogen gas in IC 59 and 63 to glow red. Their dust reflects and scatters some blue-ish white starlight. Newly discovered Objects 1, 2, and 3 appear as blue phantoms, revealing the presence of ionized oxygen. But ionized by what? Like at the bow of a speeding boat, +¦ Cassiopeia may be piling up material as the system moves through interstellar gas and dust. It follows that Object 3 may be the compressed and heated oxygen of that bow shock. Object 1 could be a planetary nebula if a central white dwarf is identified. The origins of these astronomical apparitions remain a mystery to be solved.

extraData.description: The powerful low-pressure system formed over the North Atlantic out of the remnants of Hurricane Isaias.

Hurricane IsaiasGÇöthe only Atlantic hurricane to date in 2026GÇömade landfall in Florida as a Category 2 storm on October 9. After delivering a rainy, windy blow to the U.S. Gulf Coast and drenching much of the Eastern Seaboard, the weather system had more in store.

Riding the jet stream east over the North Atlantic, IsaiasGÇÖs remnants developed into a powerful storm known as an extratropical cyclone. These low-pressure systems often feature asymmetrical, comma-shaped cloud patterns and can strike with hurricane-force winds, rain, and blizzard-like conditions.

The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-21 satellite captured this image of the extratropical cyclone brushing past Iceland on the afternoon of October 14. During its journey, the systemGÇÖs air pressure plummeted by more than 50 hectopascals over a 24-hour period, according to reportsGÇöapproximately double the criteria for explosive cyclogenesis, or bombogenesis. Some meteorologists believe the storm may have set a new October low for barometric pressure in Iceland, after correcting for altitude, likely breaking a record that has stood since 1963.

The cyclone lashed Iceland with high winds as it grazed the coast. A gust of 205 kilometers (128 miles) per hour was recorded near Eyjafjallaj+¦kull volcano in the countryGÇÖs south, while a small island just offshore saw sustained winds of 150 kilometers (93 miles) per hour. Damaging winds extended into northern parts of the country, where residents also braced for sleet and snow. Farther across the Atlantic, northwestern Scotland received gusts up to 90 kilometers (55 miles) per hour on October 14, according to news reports, resulting in cancellations on several ferry routes.

NASA Earth Observatory image by Michala Garrison, using VIIRS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE, GIBS/Worldview, and the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS). Story by Lindsey Doermann.

EditorGÇÖs Note: This article was originally published on Oct. 15, 2026, and has been updated to correct the location of the flights.

A NASA Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft will conduct low-flying research flights over farmland near Amarillo, Texas, from Thursday, Oct. 22, through Monday, Nov. 9. These flights will measure gaseous and particulate emissions from animal feeding operations.

Agricultural emissions represent an important and understudied part of EarthGÇÖs land and atmosphere systems. The FarmFlux mission will deploy more than a dozen sensors to measure ozone, methane, ammonia, particulates, and other pollutants rising from crop lands and livestock farms and their interaction with the EarthGÇÖs atmosphere. The mission is jointly led by NASAGÇÖs Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland; Colorado State University; and Boston University.

Additional low-altitude research flights with a NASA P-3 Orion aircraft are scheduled for the March to July 2027 growing season in the Midwest and CaliforniaGÇÖs Central Valley with a focus on cropland.

For more information about the FarmFlux mission, visit:

https://science.nasa.gov/mission/evs-4/farm-flux/

To expedite development of the spacecraft, NASA […]
extraData.dc:creator: Gary Daines
extraData.content:encoded:
2 min read

Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater)

Destined for Mars and beyond, NASAGÇÖs Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom will be humanityGÇÖs first fission-powered spacecraft to travel outside EarthGÇÖs orbit. Announced during NASAGÇÖs GÇ£IgnitionGÇ¥ event, this mission will demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space, and progress is underway on its key element: the nuclear power module. To expedite development of the spacecraft, NASA and its partners have mutually agreed to key contract actions that will advance the SRGÇæ1 Freedom mission. 

GÇ£These contract actions not only reduce technical risk and help us maintain momentum toward our 2028 launch, but they also strengthen collaboration across our partners,GÇ¥ said Steve Sinacore, SR-1 Freedom program director. GÇ£These actions keep SRGÇæ1 Freedom on track and ensure weGÇÖre building the strongest possible foundation for NASAGÇÖs first fissionGÇæpowered voyage beyond Earth orbit while developing technology extensible to a vibrant space nuclear future.GÇ¥ 

Sierra Lobo Inc. will provide the nuclear power moduleGÇÖs closed Brayton cycle power conversion system, which converts thermal energy from its fission reactor into electrical power needed for SR-1 FreedomGÇÖs nuclear electric propulsion demonstration. The work will be conducted under the Space Flight Systems Development and Operations Contract III, awarded in 2024, to support spaceflight hardware design, development, testing, and operations at NASAGÇÖs Glenn Research Center in Cleveland.

The power conversion system will be integrated with the fission reactor, which is being designed and developed by the Department of Energy (DOE)GÇÖs Idaho National Laboratory to complete the nuclear power module. NASA and DOE incorporate thorough safety standards throughout the design and development of the SR-1 Freedom spacecraft, including interagency safety reviews, continuous oversight by a NASA chief safety officer, regulatory compliance, and a rigorous safety design process focusing on hazards, failure tolerance, and nuclear safety. In addition, the nuclear reactor portion of SR-1 Freedom will remain inactive until the spacecraft leaves Earth orbit.

Launching in late 2028, SRGÇæ1 Freedom will deliver the SkyFall science mission, a team of three Mars helicopters evolved from the Ingenuity design, to collect scientific data, demonstrate exploration zones, and identify potential water sources. The mission will pave the way for deep space exploration and nextGÇægeneration fission-powered systems designed to keep NASAGÇÖs Moon Base operating through periods of darkness and in locations where solar power alone is not sufficient.

For information about SR-1 Freedom, visit:

https://www.nasa.gov/mission/space-reactor-1-freedom/

items.title: NASA Experimental Mars Helicopter Blade Designs Target Longer Flights

Using high-fidelity computer simulations and wind tunnel tests, engineers are reimagining the rotorcraft blades that could carry the next generation of Mars flyers.

Rotor blade cross-sections highlight the thinner profile of the roamx-0201 design (right) compared to the more traditional, rounded shape used by NASAGÇÖs Ingenuity Mars helicopter, which accomplished the first powered flight on Mars.

NASA researchers are developing the future of flight on Mars, laying the groundwork for helicopters with the ability to fly higher and farther while conducting science on the Red Planet. Using high-fidelity computer simulations and wind tunnel tests, engineers are reimagining the rotorcraft blades that could carry the next generation of Mars flyers.
 
NASAGÇÖs Ingenuity helicopter made history as the first powered aircraft to fly on another planet. The SkyFall mission, scheduled for launch in 2028, builds on that legacy with a trio of helicopters destined for Mars exploration. Both missions utilize a blade designed to operate in MarsGÇÖ thin atmosphere, with a curved edge reminiscent of but distinct from blades used on Earth.
 
Researchers are exploring unconventional blade designs that are thinner and sharper, aiming to enable future missions after Skyfall to expand their single-flight range across Mars. One team at NASAGÇÖs Ames Research Center in CaliforniaGÇÖs Silicon Valley is working with Imperial College London, United Kingdom, and Nagoya University, Japan, to test a new blade cross-section, or airfoil, that promises to significantly boost aerodynamic performance on Mars.
 
Researchers designed the new airfoil, called roamx-0201, using advanced simulations and algorithms tuned to Mars conditions, pointing researchers toward a thinner, asymmetrical shape. Subsequent wind tunnel tests showed that the optimized design boosted performance and was better able to recover in risky flight conditions.
 
Researchers used high-fidelity simulation tools to analyze the performance of the roamx-0201 airfoil and compare it to IngenuityGÇÖs capacity. They found that the redesigned blades could enable future Mars helicopters to expand the distances that can be covered in one uninterrupted flight from IngenuityGÇÖs 0.7 kilometers to as much as 18.7 kilometers while carrying scientific instruments. The findings were announced in a paper published Sept. 22 in the journal of the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics.
 
The roamxGÇæ0201 blades performed well in part because they were able to operate longer at higher speeds before experiencing a phenomenon known as GÇ£drag divergenceGÇ¥, where performance drops suddenly when the rotors approach the speed of sound, which is lower on Mars than on Earth.
 
The new blade also differs from earlier designs in how it uses turbulence to create lift. As air flows over a rotorcraft blade, it forms a thin region called the GÇ£boundary layer.GÇ¥ The new airfoil intentionally disrupts the flow of that boundary layer at the front of the airfoil directly at the leading edge to create a disturbance that, counterintuitively, pulls the blade upward to help lift the rotorcraft more effectively than with earlier designs.
 
Another challenge for rotorcraft is GÇ£stall,GÇ¥ an aerodynamic condition in which performance drops sharply and flight becomes unstable following a change in the angle of airflow. IngenuityGÇÖs blades experienced steep performance degradation at stall, but under the conditions studied, the roamx-0201 design showed significantly improved stall behavior. That means future helicopters could operate safely at a wider range of flight angles.
 
While the technology is not yet ready for Mars, tests are helping engineers understand and resolve discrepancies between computational predictions and real-world performance. Ongoing research across NASA aims to enable more efficient Mars helicopters that can fly farther, carry more payload, and unlock new science and discovery missions.

items.title: NASA Provides Progress Update on Moon Base Rovers

extraData.media:title: NASA Moon Base: Rovers and Lunar Terrain Vehicles (October 2026 Update)
extraData.content:encoded:
6 min read

Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater)

As NASA works to build the Moon Base, crewed and robotic lunar rovers will play a crucial role during early development through technology demonstrations, astronaut transport, terrain mapping, scientific investigations, and resource prospecting. Data from these early missions will inform future mobility systems and infrastructure needed for astronauts to live and work on the Moon.

On Tuesday, NASA released a Moon Base video update offering a closer look at the progress being made on the commercial lunar terrain vehicles and robotic rovers that will enable the surface mobility needed to build humanityGÇÖs first lunar outpost.

GÇ£Lunar rovers are central to our surface mobility strategy,GÇ¥ said Robert Pickle, director of the Surface Mobility Office within the agencyGÇÖs Moon Base Program. GÇ£Their performance will lay the groundwork for the mobility systems that will define the next era of exploration and ultimately determine how effectively we can build, operate, and expand the infrastructure required for longGÇæduration exploration.GÇ¥

Learn more about NASAGÇÖs VIPER

NASAGÇÖs VIPER (Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover) will embark on a mission to the lunar South Pole region in 2027 to venture into permanently shadowed craters looking for water and other valuable resources essential for sustainable exploration. 

After delivery to the lunar surface by a Blue Moon Mark 1 lander, VIPER will travel more than 18 miles (30 kilometers), collecting information about the thermal, lighting, and terrain environment in the MoonGÇÖs South Pole region. This data could provide information about the origin and distribution of water on the Moon, help determine how lunar resources could be used for the Moon Base, as well as better understand the history of the Moon, Earth, and the processes that helped shape conditions for life.

Mission operations for VIPER will be run out of NASAGÇÖs Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley where teams are simulating possible scenarios for when the rover begins its mission on the Moon.

The VIPER rover is currently at NASAGÇÖs Johnson Space Center in Houston where it is fully built and undergoing final testing before traveling to NASAGÇÖs Kennedy Space Center in Florida for launch to the Moon. 

Lunar terrain vehicles

To advance surface mobility on the Moon, NASA awarded Astrolab and Lunar Outpost task orders to build the first phase of Moon Base rovers capable of carrying crew, called lunar terrain vehicles (LTVs), that will be delivered to the Moon ahead of crewed Artemis missions. NASA awarded Blue Origin a task order to deliver the LTVs to the lunar South Pole region by 2028 through the agencyGÇÖs CLPS (Commercial Lunar Payload Services) initiative.


The LTVs will be remotely operated from Earth, traversing up to 3.7 miles (6 kilometers) a day, mapping the lunar surface to help scientists produce high-resolution maps of the region, prior to crew arriving on future missions. The rovers also will collect information to help NASA and its partners learn about operating in this extreme environment, such as data on lighting, navigation, and how well the LTVs preserve energy and function when driving in and out of permanently shadowed regions that can reach minus 334-¦F (minus 203-¦C). This will help inform Moon Base development and improve on design and capability for future mobility systems, hardware, and infrastructure. 

During missions on the lunar surface, Artemis astronauts will drive the LTVs as they explore geologically diverse areas of the lunar South Pole region, gathering geology samples to bring back to Earth for scientists to study. The LTVs will be able to support up to three moonwalks per Artemis mission, transport up to 176 pounds (80 kilograms) of lunar samples and tools, and travel up to six miles (10 kilometers) on a single battery charge.

Astrolab

AstrolabGÇÖs Crewed Lunar Vehicle 1, or CLV-1, is a rover adapted from the companyGÇÖs FLEX (Flexible Logistics and Exploration Vehicle) LTV architecture. Astrolab recently delivered a mockup of CLV-1 to Axiom Space, where NASA astronauts wore mock-ups of the Artemis lunar spacesuit and evaluated the lunar roverGÇÖs design, crew cabin, and display interfaces.

Prior to CLV-1 arriving to the Moon, Astrolab will send its first robotic rover, FLIP (FLEX Lunar Innovation Platform), to the lunar surface as a payload on Voyager TechnologiesGÇÖ Griffin Mission One scheduled to launch in late 2026. FLIP will study the environment of the South Pole and serve as a testbed for critical subsystems on CLV-1, which will include similar tires, batteries, radios, and cameras.

In the next few weeks, Astrolab engineers will head to NASAGÇÖs Glenn Research Center in Cleveland where they will use the centerGÇÖs Simulated Lunar Operations laboratory to evaluate the how CLV-1GÇÖs flexible, airless wheels perform while driving on a simulated lunar surface.

Lunar Outpost

Lunar OutpostGÇÖs Pegasus crewed LTV is a lighter, mission-ready evolution of the companyGÇÖs Eagle LTV. Prior to the award, Lunar Outpost built two mockups of Pegasus and recently delivered a third static mockup to NASAGÇÖs Johnson Space Center for crewed testing. During the test, NASA astronauts wore pressurized spacesuits and evaluated the roverGÇÖs design, usability, and crew comfort. 

In 2025, Lunar OutpostGÇÖs robotic exploration rover MAPP (Mobile Autonomous Prospecting Platform) operated at the MoonGÇÖs South Pole. During the mission, MAPP acted as a testbed and collected data, achieving flight-proven readiness for key hardware and software subsystems, like its automatic thermal control system, navigation cameras, and mission control software that will be used to remotely operate Pegasus. With a second MAPP rover scheduled to launch in early 2027, Lunar Outpost is advancing many of the key technologies that are directly transferable to Pegasus.

In the next few weeks, Lunar Outpost teams also will head to NASA Glenn to test and evaluate the soil mechanics, traction, and mobility of PegasusGÇÖ spring mesh tires.

In the coming months, both Astrolab and Lunar Outpost will test drivable LTV mockups with NASA crew to evaluate how the rovers drive and operate in a simulated lunar environment. Lunar Outpost is scheduled to complete the preliminary design review of their LTV in October, and Astrolab is scheduled to complete their preliminary design review by the end of December. Both companies are on schedule to deliver the flight-ready hardware to NASA at the end of 2027.

As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions near the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before. In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on the agencyGÇÖs foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

To learn more about the Moon Base, visit:

https://www.nasa.gov/moonbase

extraData.title: NASA Welcomes Uzbekistan as Newest Artemis Accords Signatory
category: Office of International and Interagency Relations (OIIR)
extraData.content:encoded:
The Republic of Uzbekistan became the 77th signatory of the Artemis Accords during a ceremony in Samarkand on Monday, committing to the practical principles that guide safe, transparent, and responsible civil space exploration.

GÇ£Uzbekistan joins the Artemis Accords at a pivotal moment,GÇ¥ said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson. GÇ£President Trump has directed NASA to build a Moon Base and establish an enduring presence on the lunar surface. As we put the principles of the Artemis Accords into practice, we are expanding opportunities for like-minded nations around the world to contribute to humanity’s return to the Moon. Uzbekistan is a welcome addition to this growing coalition.GÇ¥

Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Uzbekistan Bakhtiyor Saidov signed the Artemis Accords on behalf of the country. The signing took place during a visit by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Uzbekistan has increasingly engaged with NASA and the broader international space community through its development of a national space program aimed at advancing Uzbekistan’s space industry and participation in global space forums. Uzbek students also are working to develop and launch the countryGÇÖs first CubeSat, or small satellite technology demonstration, by 2028.

In early October, NASA officials met with representatives from UzbekistanGÇÖs Ministry of Digital Technologies and Uzbekistan’s space agency, Uzcosmos, during the 2026 International Astronautical Congress in Antalya, T++rkiye, where the two sides discussed civil space cooperation and opportunities for increased engagement. Uzbekistan is scheduled to host the annual global space event in 2028.

In 2020, NASA and the State Department joined with seven other founding nations to establish the Artemis Accords, responding to the growing interest in lunar activities by both governments and private companies. They introduced the first set of practical principles aimed at enhancing the safety and coordination between nations as they explore the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

Signing the Artemis Accords means committing to explore peaceably and transparently, to render aid to those in need, to enable access to scientific data that all of humanity can learn from, to ensure activities do not interfere with those of others, and to preserve historically significant sites and artifacts by developing best practices for space exploration for the benefit of all. 

More countries are expected to sign the Artemis Accords in the months and years ahead, as NASA continues its work to establish a safe, peaceful, and prosperous future in space. 

Learn more about the Artemis Accords at: 

https://www.nasa.gov/artemis-accords

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

An Anticrepuscular Rainbow Fan

Explanation: This is an unusual rainbow. For one thing, the rainbow is not complete, appearing only in a sunlit fan GÇö but that by itself is not very unusual. What is most unusual is the fake location of the Sun. The Sun appears to be toward the front, just below those hills GÇö but it is not. That is not how rainbows work. Rainbows involve a backward reflection from falling rain, so that the Sun must really be behind you. In this case, gaps between clouds near the setting Sun allowed rays to cross the entire sky and appear to converge in front, an unusual phenomenon called anticrepuscular rays. The photo was taken with a phone last week at sunset in Presenzano, Italy. The seemingly reverse rainbow was noticed when hanging up laundry.

Humans are exerting increasing influence over how water moves through lakes, rivers, soil, and the subsurface, and a new NASA study shows where those effects are greatest. Using more than two decades of satellite measurements of subtle changes in EarthGÇÖs gravity, the researchers sharpened the picture of howGÇöand whyGÇöterrestrial water storage has changed.

This map encapsulates their findings, depicting changes in terrestrial water storage from April 2002 to November 2025. Beyond the influence of climate variability, the scientists identified 40 regions where the changes also aligned with human activities such as irrigation, reservoir impoundment, and land-use change. These activities were significantly related to terrestrial water storage trends on every nonpolar continent except Australia.

In some areas, the effects of human activities were especially strong. GÇ£In four continental regions, an anthropogenic variable showed a stronger relationship with the storage trends than any climate variable did,GÇ¥ said Mary Michael OGÇÖNeill, a hydrologist at NASAGÇÖs Goddard Space Flight Center and lead author of the study.

They include well-known spots such as CaliforniaGÇÖs Central Valley and northern India, where farmersGÇÖ heavy reliance on groundwater has drawn down storageGÇöin IndiaGÇÖs case, faster than earlier estimates suggested. Elsewhere, some types of farming and water management appear to have done the opposite.

Gravity as a Water Gauge

The data behind the map come from the GRACE (Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment) and GRACE-FO (GRACE Follow-On) missions, each of which consists of two satellites that fly in tandem. As the lead satellite passes over an area with greater mass, the slight change in gravity tugs at it, and instruments aboard the satellites measure the change in distance between them. Since water and ice are heavy and shift around regularly, scientists can use GRACE data to infer gains and losses.

The satellitesGÇÖ data are typically processed into monthly maps that show broad patterns of water storage. But over more than 20 years, the satellites have passed over most of the planet many times. By combining all of those passes, the researchers could map long-term water trends with five to 10 times more spatial detail than previous analyses. The tradeoff was a loss of temporal detail. They then applied statistical techniques to weigh the importance of various anthropogenic and climatic factors in the storage trends and to pinpoint where human activities may have contributed.

The improved spatial resolution uncovered some human impacts that had not been previously detected, said Matthew Rodell, deputy director of Earth Sciences for Hydrosphere, Biosphere, and Geophysics at Goddard and one of the studyGÇÖs authors. The analysis also showed that some known trends were stronger than previously realized.

Where the Water Went

Across several continents, groundwater-irrigated farmland was strongly associated with declines in terrestrial water storage. In North America, these declines appeared in CaliforniaGÇÖs Central Valley, the southern High Plains of the U.S., and Chihuahua, Mexico, where long-term droughts have increased farmersGÇÖ reliance on groundwater. Groundwater pumping also drove declines in northern India, where the refined analysis showed a steeper downward trend than previously realized. Consistent with previous findings, retreating Himalayan glaciers accounted for only 15 percent of the decline there.

Other types of agriculture had a different relationship with water storage trends. In parts of sub-Saharan Africa, for example, some increases occurred where rainfed cropland has expanded. There, swaths of native savanna were replaced by millet cultivation throughout the study period, and water tables rose despite below-average precipitation. A similar pattern emerged in northern BrazilGÇÖs Maranh+úo state, where soybean fields have replaced forests and shrublands. The resulting water storage trend might be explained in part by the efficient water use of cereal and legume plants and by Indigenous practices that help direct water into shallow aquifers, the researchers said.

Water storage and diversion projects also came into focus on the new map. Hundreds of large reservoirs were filled during the study period, the authors note, but the coarse spatial resolution of gravity measurements previously made them difficult to track. In the new analysis, the Boguchany Reservoir on RussiaGÇÖs Angara River, the second-largest reservoir filled in the 21st century, produced the strongest water storage trend in nonpolar northern Asia.

The map also resolves smaller reservoirs and other hydrologic engineering projects. The Karakum Desert in Turkmenistan registered water storage gains stemming from the long, largely unlined Karakum Canal running through it. The canal diverts river water to support desert agriculture, but enough seeps into the ground during its journey to alter the water picture in the desert. The mapGÇÖs finer resolution allows for better monitoring of such hydrologic changes in remote areas where other measurement options may be limited.

Moving forward, OGÇÖNeill wants to capture how dams, diversions, irrigation, and other controls on EarthGÇÖs water affect storage downstream, and to disentangle the influence of local and non-local activities. GÇ£IGÇÖd also like to recover more of the temporal picture,GÇ¥ she said. One way to do that is by combining the higher-resolution data with standard monthly products or by applying the recent technique over shorter timeframes. GÇ£This could help track how localized trends evolve in response to specific events like droughts or policy changes.GÇ¥

Astronaut photograph ISS065-E-111045 was acquired on June 13, 2021, with a Nikon D5 digital camera using a focal length of 1,150 millimeters. It is provided by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit at NASA Johnson Space Center. The image was taken by a member of the Expedition 65 crew. The image has been cropped and enhanced to improve contrast, and lens artifacts have been removed. The International Space Station Program supports the laboratory as part of the ISS National Lab to help astronauts take pictures of Earth that will be of the greatest value to scientists and the public, and to make those images freely available on the internet. Additional images taken by astronauts and cosmonauts can be viewed at the NASA/JSC Gateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth. Story by Lindsey Doermann.

Curiosity Blog, Sols 5036-5042: Watching the Clouds Go By

Written by Alex Innanen, Atmospheric Scientist at York University

Earth planning date: Friday, Oct. 9, 2026

Happy New Mars Year! We mark the start of a new year on Mars at the beginning of the northern hemisphere spring, or the vernal equinox. We then keep track of the seasons by counting degrees of solar longitude GÇö each season is 90 degrees as Mars completes the whole 360 degrees of its orbit. The start of Mars year 39 at a solar longitude of 0 degrees (or Ls=0-¦, pronounced GÇ£ell-sub-ess-zeroGÇ¥ if you want to sound like a Martian) came at the end of September on Earth. The new year also means itGÇÖs now autumn in Gale Crater, just south of the equator.

As Michelle talked about last week, we rang in the Martian new year with our drill campaign at GÇ£Basque Lakes.GÇ¥ This week was dedicated to wrapping up drill activities before we drive away on the weekend. After the team got a chance to see the results of last weekGÇÖs lab activities, the SAM team decided on an additional GCMS (Gas Chromatograph/Mass Spectrometry) experiment. While GCMS tends to be an energy-intensive activity, we had four whole sols in MondayGÇÖs plan to play with, so we still had room for a slew of remote-sensing activities from Mastcam and ChemCam and contact science of the drill tailings GÇö the bits of rock and minerals that are left over from our drill sample. This weekendGÇÖs plan gives us a couple more sols to wrap up drill activities at Basque Lakes and collect any last contact- or remote-science targets we want here before we begin a drive back toward the neat crystal forms we saw in the GÇ£Chiu ChiuGÇ¥ region.

While all this is happening, the atmosphere around us continues to go through its seasonal changes. Autumn means the return of high-altitude twilight clouds, which the low sun angle at sunset illuminates beautifully. While twilight cloud activity will pick up as the autumn progresses, our late afternoon cloud movies on Wednesday of this week already caught our first high-altitude clouds of the season, as you can see at the top of this post. Most of the clouds we tend to see at Gale Crater are suboptical, or too thin to be seen with either human eyes or with CuriosityGÇÖs robotic GÇ£eyes,GÇ¥ but these twilight clouds are bright enough that we can see them in the raw Navcam images. IGÇÖm looking forward to another Martian autumn of watching all these different clouds go by.

extraData.title: NASA Improves Shock, Vibration Analysis
extraData.content:encoded:
Rockets vibrate, shake, and flex intensely as they climb into space, and spacecraft packed with delicate scientific instruments must survive those forces. Before any rocket leaves the ground, NASA engineers work to predict how those stresses will affect every part of a spacecraft.

To do that, engineers in the Dynamic Environments Group with NASAGÇÖs Launch Services Program Office at the agencyGÇÖs Kennedy Space Center in Florida have streamlined how they ensure spacecraft and rockets can withstand harsh vibration, shock, stress, or other physical forces, strengthening mission safety in the process.

Using a commercial digital software tool in a new way, the engineers developed a standardized modeling workflow for finite element modeling to strengthen shock and vibration analysis and ensure hardware is prepared for the extreme environments of launch and ascent.

GÇ£This computer-based method helps predict how rockets and spacecraft behave under extreme conditions before hardware is built and helps identify weak spots and potential failure risks early so the team can address the findings,GÇ¥ said Brian Beaver, chief of the Flight Analysis Division with the Launch Services Program Office at NASA Kennedy.

The team recently used the software for the first time while certifying a commercial launch providerGÇÖs rocket selected for a NASA mission. The commercial partner provided vibration testing but not shock testing. The Dynamic Environments Group determined shock testing was needed and used a template the group created to run what-if comparisons, visualize structural behavior, and answer complex questions that would have required extensive manual modeling in the past. The team verified the companyGÇÖs testing results for flight environments, and the analysis provided new insights addressing shock during transport.

GÇ£We are using a tool thatGÇÖs existed for decades, but itGÇÖs not normally used by the dynamic environments disciplines,GÇ¥ said Alex Hardt, aerospace engineer with the Launch Services Program Office at NASA Kennedy. GÇ£But weGÇÖre changing that. WeGÇÖre using it in a relatively new area of dynamics.GÇ¥

Although rockets and spacecraft are designed to absorb shocks and vibrations, those forces can cause wear and tear or potentially flight failures, especially during launch and ascent.

GÇ£We define how severe the random vibration levels and shock levels are, and then we verify that all the parts going on future rockets have been tested to those levels, maximizing their longevity,GÇ¥ Hardt said.

Software time saver

For decades, engineers have estimated shock and vibration environments using rules of thumb or by scaling previous data to estimate how each rocket component or spacecraft equipment would be impacted once assembled and flown. The approach worked, but relied heavily on engineering judgment and simple approximations drawn from past missions.

Because most dynamic environments engineers use finite element modeling tools infrequently, they often need to re-learn complex workflows. The software replaces older tools and provides a standard template that guides engineers more quickly and thoroughly through vibration profiles and shock conditions.

Finite element analysis is a powerful simulation technique that breaks a complex structure into smaller components so computers can accurately predict how a spacecraft or rocket could respond to specific forces or launch environments. This is important because issues can be addressed on the ground; once the rocket leaves the launch pad, most problems cannot be repaired or corrected, making early identification essential.

GÇ£WeGÇÖve used it to get really valuable insight very quickly into verifying a providerGÇÖs system,GÇ¥ Hardt said. GÇ£ItGÇÖs already provided some really deep insight into something that normally takes a lot of effort.GÇ¥

Hardt says having the ability to visualize non-intuitive dynamics problems using finite element models also highlights the softwareGÇÖs valuable impact on learning, efficiency, and alignment with NASAGÇÖs people focused culture. The workflow can help the engineers share knowledge, refine assessments with additional flight data, and increase proficiency with modeling tools. This capability already has saved months by allowing the team to run analysis independently without having to request and wait for analysis reports or data, and by helping them identify risks that weren’t previously considered.

NASAGÇÖs Launch Services Program Office is responsible for launching rockets delivering spacecraft that observe the Earth, visit other planets and explore the universe, from weather satellites to space telescopes to Mars rovers. The team is constantly adopting new tools like this to give the agency the highest practical chance of success for each mission.

Astronomy Picture of the Day

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

Sonified: Eagle Nebula Pillars

Explanation: Yes, but have you ever experienced the Eagle Nebula with your ears? The famous nebula M16 is best known for the feast it gives your eyes, highlighting bright young stars forming deep inside dark towering structures. These light-years long columns of cold gas and dust are some 6,500 light-years distant toward the constellation of the Serpent (Serpens). Sculpted and eroded by the energetic ultraviolet light and powerful winds from M16GÇÿs cluster of massive stars, the cosmic pillars themselves are destined for destruction. But the turbulent environment of star formation within M16, whose spectacular details are captured in this combined Hubble (visible) and Chandra (X-ray) image, is likely similar to the environment that formed our own Sun. In the featured video, listen for stars and dust sounding off as the line of sonification moves left to right, with vertical position determining pitch.

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

3D 67P

Explanation: Put on your red/blue glasses and float next to the jagged and double-lobed nucleus of Churyumov-Gerasimenko, also known as Comet 67P . The stereo anaglyph was created by combining two images from the Rosetta spacecraftGÇÖs narrow angle OSIRIS camera taken on July 25, 2015 from a distance of 184 kilometers. Numerous jets are emanating from the small solar system worldGÇÖs active surface near its closest approach to the Sun. The larger lobe is around 4 kilometers in diameter, joined to a smaller, 2.5 kilometer diameter lobe by a narrow neck. RosettaGÇÖs mission to the comet ended in September 2016 when the spacecraft was commanded to a controlled impact with the cometGÇÖs surface . Keep those 3D glasses on though. You can check out a catalog of nearly 1400 stereo anaglyphs created from Rosetta image data on this website.

items.title: NASA Names Stephen Cash Marshall Space Flight Center Director

extraData.description: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has named Stephen Cash director of the agencyGÇÖs Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, effective Monday, Oct. 19. Cash, a veteran NASA engineer and aerospace executive, returns to lead the center where he began his career more than four decades ago. GÇ£Marshall contributions to NASA’s missions are historic and it’s […]
extraData.dc:creator: Gerelle Q. Dodson
extraData.content:encoded:
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has named Stephen Cash director of the agencyGÇÖs Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, effective Monday, Oct. 19. Cash, a veteran NASA engineer and aerospace executive, returns to lead the center where he began his career more than four decades ago.

GÇ£Marshall contributions to NASA’s missions are historic and it’s no question why it’s the Center of Excellence for propulsion,GÇ¥ said Isaacman. GÇ£Steve Cash is a Marshall legend, has spent his career around the hardware, the people and has been in the seat before making the decisions when human spaceflight is on the line. As Marshall continues its critical role in Artemis and takes on new challenges in advanced propulsion, nuclear power, and the systems that will carry us deeper into the solar system, Steve brings the experience, technical judgment, and mission focus needed to lead the center into that next chapter. I am also grateful to Rae Ann Meyer for the leadership she has provided to Marshall during this transition and for her continued service to NASA.GÇ¥ 

GÇ£Leading a NASA center requires a commitment to its people and to the technical capabilities entrusted to them,GÇ¥ said Amit Kshatriya, NASA associate administrator and chief engineer. GÇ£Steve understands that the jewel of Marshall is its workforce and that engineering excellence is sustained by giving talented people the opportunity to design, build, test, and learn through hands-on work. As Marshall continues strengthening the manufacturing, structural loads and dynamics, and propulsion capabilities that underpin NASAGÇÖs exploration enterprise, SteveGÇÖs leadership will help ensure the workforce has opportunities to develop and apply the expertise needed to deliver the agencyGÇÖs most ambitious missions.GÇ¥

As center director, Cash will lead one of NASAGÇÖs largest field centers, overseeing a workforce of more than 5,000 civil service and contractor employees and a broad portfolio of propulsion, space systems, scientific research, and technology development activities. Marshall plays a critical role in NASAGÇÖs Artemis program, including the development of NASAGÇÖs SLS (Space Launch System) rocket, management of the Human Landing System Program, as well as other capabilities supporting sustained exploration of the Moon and future missions to Mars. Further, Marshall plays a key role in the advancement of nuclear power and propulsion, an area of focus that is expected to grow as NASA works towards sending the first humans to Mars.

GÇ£It is a profound honor to be back home at the Marshall Space Flight Center,GÇ¥ said Cash. GÇ£I am humbled to stand alongside the brilliant minds here as we continue to turn the impossible into everyday history.GÇ¥

Cash began his NASA career at Marshall in 1982 and spent 34 years with the agency, holding senior engineering and management positions supporting some of the nationGÇÖs most significant human spaceflight programs.

During his NASA career, Cash served as manager of MarshallGÇÖs Space Shuttle Propulsion Office, overseeing critical propulsion systems supporting shuttle through its final missions. He later served as director of MarshallGÇÖs Safety and Mission Assurance Directorate from 2011 until his retirement in 2016, providing leadership in safety, reliability, and quality engineering to support mission success across the center.

Following his retirement from NASA, Cash continued his work in the aerospace industry, including serving as vice president for advanced space systems at Axient, supporting the development and execution of major spaceflight programs. In 2024, he was inducted into the Alabama Engineering Hall of Fame in recognition of his contributions to engineering and the nation’s space program.

Cash succeeds Rae Ann Meyer, who has served as MarshallGÇÖs acting center director since September 2025. Meyer, who previously served as MarshallGÇÖs deputy center director and associate director, has provided leadership and continuity across the centerGÇÖs programs and operations during her tenure as acting director. Meyer will return to her role as Deputy Center Director.

Established in 1960, Marshall has played a central role in American space exploration for more than six decades, from developing the Saturn rockets that carried astronauts to the Moon during Apollo to advancing the propulsion systems, infrastructure, and technologies supporting the next era of human spaceflight.

For more information about NASAGÇÖs Marshall Space Flight Center, visit:

https://www.nasa.gov/marshall

-end-

extraData.dc:creator: Jason Costa
extraData.content:encoded:
3 Min Read

I Am Artemis: Allison Mjoen

As the supercooled propellant flowed into the core stage, and NASAGÇÖs SLS (Space Launch System) rocket roared to life, Allison Mjoen and her family watched with awe and pride. Mjoen, NASAGÇÖs operations manager for the agencyGÇÖs Exploration Ground Systems Program, helped shape the systems and ground operations that will one day send humans back to the Moon. Over her 20-year career at NASAGÇÖs Kennedy Space Center in Florida, she supported missions across the Space Shuttle Program, the International Space Station, and now she is applying that experience to Artemis.

April 1, 2026, was a bright, crystal-clear day along the Florida Space Coast. The sunlight seemed to sharpen every color along the horizon. As Mjoen and her children counted down and the crowdGÇÖs voices rose around them, the rumble of the SLS rocket intensified beneath their feet. For her children, it was the chance to see what their mom had helped make possible. For Mjoen, it was a moment she would never forget.

That moment also offered a pause for reflection on the work that led her there. As the spacecraft offline operations manager, Mjoen coordinates the work that happens long before launch day. By supporting the ground systemsGÇÖ senior vehicle operations manager, Matt Czech, she develops integration plans and oversees ground operations for Artemis vehicle processing, focusing on booster and Orion spacecraft operations.

Mjoen began her career as a flight crew systems engineer with United Space Alliance supporting the Space Shuttle Program. Her team handled mission-specific cabin configurations, including the food, spacesuits, cargo, and payloads astronauts needed aboard the shuttle.

After the Space Shuttle Program retired, she supported the International Space Station Program as a payload integration engineer. In this role, she connected experiment investigators with the organizations developing their hardware. NASAGÇÖs Hubble Spies SpiralGÇÖs Edge

This NASA Hubble Space Telescope image features the edge-on, intermediate spiral galaxy NGC 1827, located roughly 37 million light-years away in the constellation Columba, the Dove. Hubble captured the image as part of a survey looking at 260 satellite galaxies around 22 Milky Way-like host galaxies within a radius of about 32 million light-years from Earth. Hubble has already observed 111 of these satellite galaxies. The remaining galaxies will take an additional 149 Hubble orbits, one orbit for each galaxy, to observe.

The image, taken with HubbleGÇÖs Advanced Camera for Surveys, reveals bright-blue regions along the galaxyGÇÖs disk dotted with dark dust lanes where new stars are likely forming. A bright foreground star appears just to the left of the galaxyGÇÖs bright central bulge but is located between us and the galaxy. Its four diffraction spikes are the result of light bending around the internal supports that hold HubbleGÇÖs secondary mirror.

Low-mass galaxies like the ones in this Hubble observing program provide a way to test the predictions of cosmological models on small scales, which struggle to match observations. The data Hubble gathers will help us better understand and characterize the properties of low-mass galaxies in Milky Way-like systems, allowing researchers to refine cosmological models.

Astronomy Picture of the Day

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

Chasing the International Space Station

Explanation: Blasting into the predawn sky on Tuesday, October 13, a Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft are headed for low Earth orbit in this stunning timelapse video captured from Indian Harbour Beach, Florida. Starting with a launch from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Falcon and Dragon are chasing the International Space Station on NASAGÇÖs 35th Commercial Resupply Services mission. On cue, the space station itself enters the frame from the top. Almost 8 seconds into the 30 second timelapse. the bright streak of the ISS appears heading GÇ£downGÇ¥ toward the horizon. The first and second stages of the Falcon 9 are separating as the spectacular exhaust plume jellyfish grows, already catching the light of the rising Sun. The visible sequence of first stage boost back, re-entry, and landing burns begins around 20 seconds into the video. With the second stage following the ISS toward the distant horizon, the jellyfish plume continues to drift in the predawn sky, even after the successful first stage landing at planet EarthGÇÖs Landing Zone 40.

August 2026 Composite
October 11, 2026


August 2026 Composite

October 11, 2026


Lights around Pensacola, Florida, and along the U.S. Route 98 corridor toward Destin appear sharply reduced on October 11, 2026 (right), compared with typical conditions in August 2026 (left), suggesting widespread power outages after Hurricane Isaias. Images are from NASAGÇÖs Black Marble HD product.

After a quiet start to the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, Isaias became the seasonGÇÖs first hurricane on October 8 as it tracked toward the U.S. Gulf Coast. The storm brought heavy rain and flash flooding to parts of the Southeast, including Alabama and the Florida Panhandle, and winds that toppled trees and downed power lines, leaving many people in the dark.

Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on the evening of October 9 as a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105 miles (170 kilometers) per hour. Gusts topped 100 miles per hour along a corridor west of the stormGÇÖs center, according to the National Weather Service, with preliminary reports showing a 117-mile-per-hour gust in Oriole Beach and a 102-mile-per-hour gust at Pensacola City Hall.

These areas of high winds overlapped a broader area west of the stormGÇÖs eye where satellite images showed substantial decreases in nighttime lights. The image pair above shows nighttime lights before and after the storm. The left image is a composite of August 2026 data representing typical conditions, and the right image shows lights on October 11, after most of the stormGÇÖs clouds had cleared.

The data depicted in the images, provided by Ranjay Shrestha of NASAGÇÖs Black Marble science team, come from the Black Marble HD product. The product uses data from the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-20 satellite, which has a day-night band that detects light emitted and reflected at night. The team processed the data to account for changes in the landscape, the atmosphere, and phase of the Moon, and to filter out stray light that does not come from electric lights. Dark gray, hash-marked areas show where clouds prevented VIIRS from collecting data. The nighttime lights are shown over a base map from the Landsat 9 satellite.

GÇ£Standard Black Marble nighttime lights imagery, available through NASA Worldview, provides a broad picture of the stormGÇÖs immediate impacts,GÇ¥ Shrestha said. GÇ£Black Marble HD takes this a step further by allowing us to visualize these changes at a much finer spatial scale.GÇ¥

At these finer scales, the images reveal lights decreasing sharply around parts of Pensacola, Florida, and along the U.S. Route 98 corridor toward Destin, suggesting widespread power disruptions. Shrestha also pointed out pockets where lights persisted, including Pensacola International Airport, Pensacola Christian College, and parts of downtown Pensacola. GÇ£These patterns could reflect backup power systems, differences in electrical infrastructure, or areas that maintained electricity during the storm, although the imagery alone cannot confirm the underlying reasons,GÇ¥ he said.




October 11, 2026
October 12, 2026


October 11, 2026

October 12, 2026


Widespread outages darken the region around Pensacola, Florida, and along the U.S. Route 98 corridor toward Destin on October 11, 2026 (left). By October 12 (right), lights have returned to some affected areas. Images are from NASAGÇÖs Black Marble HD product.

Black Marble HD images also reveal the pace and spatial patterns of recovery. The image pair above compares the same October 11 view (left) with one from October 12 (right), when lights had begun to return to some affected areas. By October 14, lighting patterns looked similar to pre-storm conditions.

GÇ£Understanding where recovery is progressing and where disruptions persist can help emergency responders and decision makers identify areas that may require additional attention, prioritize resources, and assess the effectiveness of restoration efforts,GÇ¥ Shrestha said.

Black Marble data complement ground-based outage reports rather than replace them, offering a more comprehensive view of disastersGÇÖ impacts and recovery. GÇ£Ultimately, this is where the value of Black Marble lies: turning nighttime Earth observations into actionable insights that support informed decisions and help bridge the gap between Earth science and action,GÇ¥ Shrestha said.

The NASA Disasters Program, in coordination with FEMA and the USGS Coastal Storms Team, is supporting the Alabama Red Cross and the Alabama Emergency Management AgencyGÇÖs response to Hurricane Isaias. The team will be posting maps and data products on its open-access mapping portal as new information becomes available.

NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Black Marble HD data courtesy of Ranjay Shrestha/NASAGÇÖs Goddard Space Flight Center and Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Story by Kathryn Hansen.
