extraData.content:encoded:
NASA is playing an important role in JAXAGÇÖs (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) MMX (Martian Moons eXploration) mission, to advance our understanding of MarsGÇÖ moons and build on the agencyGÇÖs long history of exploring the Red Planet.

The mission aims to characterize and determine the origin of MarsGÇÖ moons Phobos and Deimos and deliver a sample of Phobos to Earth. The MMX spacecraft is targeting launch from JAXAGÇÖs Tanegashima Space Center in Japan at 3:41 p.m. EDT on Monday, Oct. 19 (4:41 a.m. JST on Tuesday, Oct. 20).

GÇ£The samples from MMX will bring forth paradigm-shifting science on the Mars system for generations to come, especially as NASA prepares to send the first humans to Mars,GÇ¥ said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. GÇ£The NASA-JAXA sample curation partnership is extremely valuable, and I am proud that NASA Science is supporting MMX sample curation and will be sharing portions of these samples for study as we continue to expand humanityGÇÖs understanding of the universe for the benefit of all.GÇ¥

NASAGÇÖs contributions to the mission include the Mars-moon Exploration with Gamma rays and Neutrons (MEGANE) spectrograph instrument, the Pneumatic Sampler (P-Sampler) technology demonstration, and communications and navigation support from the agencyGÇÖs Deep Space Network, as well as funding United States scientists participating on the MMX science team.

Scientists have long debated the origin of MarsGÇÖ two moons. The data and samples collected by the MMX mission will help answer essential questions about the origins of these moons and the history of the solar system.

GÇ£Phobos and Deimos may be the remains of a massive impact on Mars that sent material into orbit around the planet, or they could be ancient asteroids that were captured by MarsGÇÖ gravity billions of years ago,GÇ¥ said Tom Statler, MMX program executive and program scientist at NASA Headquarters. GÇ£Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds.GÇ¥

The MEGANE (pronounced meh-GAH-nay, the Japanese word for eyeglasses) spectrograph will help scientists GÇ£seeGÇ¥ what Phobos is made of by measuring neutrons and gamma rays emitted from the moonGÇÖs surface and determining its chemical elemental composition, which will provide important clues about its origin.

Mounted on one of the spacecraftGÇÖs landing legs, the P-Sampler is designed to collect a ground sample from Phobos. The system gathers surface material using bursts of high-pressure nitrogen gas, complementing JAXAGÇÖs C-Sampler, which will extract cores from a few inches deeper. NASA will obtain and curate about 15% of the total returned sample at the agencyGÇÖs Johnson Space Center Astromaterials Lab in Houston, making it available for research for decades.

Another key part of NASAGÇÖs contribution to MMX is its scientific partnership with JAXA. NASA-supported researchers are working alongside international colleagues to help reveal the story of Phobos and will use mission data and returned samples to uncover new clues about the moonGÇÖs origin and the evolution of the Mars system.

The MMX spacecraft will arrive at Mars in August 2027 to begin its survey of the Red PlanetGÇÖs two moons. After surveying Phobos in detail, the spacecraft will collect a sample of the moonGÇÖs surface no earlier than December 2028 and deliver it to Earth in 2031.

The MEGANE instrument was developed by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory. Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin company, developed the spacecraftGÇÖs pneumatic sampler mechanism. NASAGÇÖs contributions to the MMX mission were developed under the agencyGÇÖs Discovery Program. The Discovery Program is managed by NASAGÇÖs Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, for the agencyGÇÖs Science Mission Directorate in Washington.

For more information about the MMX mission, visit:

https://science.nasa.gov/mission/mmx

extraData.content:encoded:
6 Min Read

NASA Satellites Observe Historic 2026 El Ni+¦o

A phenomenon rarer than a solar eclipse and more powerful than any single storm system is unfolding this fall, and NASA is tracking it closely.

El Ni+¦o is a natural climate pattern that emerges roughly every two to seven years marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific. NASA scientists are keeping watch as it flips trade winds, redistributes ocean heat, scrambles rain patterns, and raises sea surface height across parts of the Pacific.

As of October, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has said that thereGÇÖs an 83% chance that the strongest El Ni+¦o since 1950 is currently unfolding. People around the world, including farmers, firefighters, and coastal communities, are already experiencing the effects in different ways.

Follow along with these maps as NASA tracks El Ni+¦o from its epicenter in the equatorial Pacific Ocean.

Sea surface height in flux

One of the first clues appeared in satellite imagery in January 2026, when a swell of warm water called a Kelvin wave was spotted near Micronesia in the western Pacific. Kelvin waves are slow-moving pulses of water thousands of miles long. Like underwater freeways, they transfer heat from west to east across the Pacific. The warm water heats the air directly above it, making it rise. The change in air pressures weakens or even reverses the trade winds that typically blow in the opposing direction, from the Americas toward Asia, causing sea levels in the eastern Pacific to rise further, and waters to warm even more. This chain reaction signifies the start of an El Ni+¦o.

The map above shows that by early April, those Kelvin waves had reached the eastern Pacific, and sea surface temperatures had begun to warm. Warm water expands in volume, elevating local sea levels in some areas by as much as 1 to 1.3 feet (30 to 40 centimeters). The higher-than-normal water can be seen sloshing toward South America then moving up the coast to California. Sea levels that are six to eight inches (15 to 20 centimeters) lower than normal are visible around Indonesia and northern Australia.

GÇ£Kelvin waves are like the heartbeat of El Ni+¦o,GÇ¥ said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASAGÇÖs Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. GÇ£And our sea level satellites let us peer into the ocean and watch every beat.GÇ¥

Scientists have used satellite altimetry to track the height of the ocean with ultraprecision since 1993. That unbroken data record continues today with the Sentinel-6 satellites. State-of-the-art radar altimeters aboard these satellites survey millions of square miles of ocean in a single day, complementing NOAAGÇÖs fleet of ocean sensors and buoys drifting and diving through the water below.

Warming Pacific waters

Warmer-than-normal seawater is one of the best-known indicators of El Ni+¦o. Already, sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific are about 3 degrees Fahrenheit (1.7 degrees Celsius) warmer than the long-term average and could jump another fraction of a degree in the coming months, Willis said.

Satellites carrying microwave and infrared radiometers can see through and around clouds to measure heat energy at the sea surface. Satellites in 2026 mapped the band of warmer-than-normal water as it expanded throughout the spring. The band, seen in dark red, stretches for millions of square miles from the heart of the Pacific to the coast of South America. Ocean temperatures can influence weather patterns around the world. Air above the waterGÇÖs surface carries heat and moisture into the atmosphere, seeding rainstorms and rearranging weather patterns across the globe.

Ocean gets bluer

El Ni+¦oGÇÖs warm waters also change the color of the ocean. A NASA satellite is tracking these subtle shifts in hues, as equatorial Pacific waters have become measurably more blue over the last several months.

GÇ£Some people think of water as being just blue, but itGÇÖs amazing the multitude of colors the ocean can be,GÇ¥ said Matthew Kehrli, a lead research scientist for the PACE (Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem) satellite team at NASAGÇÖs Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.

This spectrum is in part thanks to microscopic plants called phytoplankton, which form the basis of the marine food web. There are thousands of different species of phytoplankton, which come in shades like teal, brown, or green. This year, in areas of the Pacific Ocean along the equator that are typically lush with phytoplankton and greener as a result, these hues are waning.

This is an expected effect of El Ni+¦o. Phytoplankton thrive in cool, nutrient-rich waters, but during an El Ni+¦o, the weakening trade winds reduce the upwelling of nutrient-rich deep water to the ocean surface. With limited food supply, phytoplankton abundance drops. This decline can trigger cascading effects across the marine food web, forcing other marine life to relocate to new feeding grounds.

This yearGÇÖs El Ni+¦o is the first since PACE launched in 2024, providing new views of the phenomenon. The Ocean Color Instrument aboard PACE observes the ocean in hyperspectral color GÇö across several hundred different wavelengths of visible, near-infrared, and ultraviolet light GÇö monitoring phytoplankton and other ocean-color changes in near-real time. With PACE data, researchers calculate the average color of the ocean, simplifying spectra of light into a single number, known as apparent visible wavelength.

The 2026 map above shows the green area along the equator in the western Pacific Ocean shrink as a bluer shade fills in, indicating fewer phytoplankton. In contrast, the map from 2025 shows how the green-hued section stays steady over time.

GÇ£You have expectations of what you would think would happen,GÇ¥ Kehrli said. GÇ£But to visually see the results with the data products that youGÇÖre working with in real time is gratifying.GÇ¥

NASA scientists will continue to monitor the signs and impacts of this El Ni+¦o with its fleet of Earth-observing satellites.

GÇ£El Ni+¦o touches almost all of us in some way every time it occurs,GÇ¥ Willis said. GÇ£While many have seen what it can do, we look to the ocean to understand why.GÇ¥
